items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: Well, that began with an invitation from a gentleman from Princeton University, a Dr. Monroe Berger, whom I'm sure you've met.

ctx.x: And they had Leon Abbey. They had someone else whose name I can't remember at the moment. I can see his face before me, but I can't remember the name. MR. BERGER: Was the music you played there in this early time, early in the sense that it was in the early thirties, was that the kind of music that would be called Swing?

items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: Monroe Burger -- that I heard -- someone had asked me to go hear, and after I listened to a few sets and we left, he said, 'What did you think of him' and I said, 'He dazzled me, but he didn't move me.'

ctx.x: Like Untouchable? Yeah, I don't know -- it's very hard to criticize anything that he did. When he came on the scene, he was such a blockbuster. I mean, no one had heard anything like Tatum. And like I heard a musician, as I had mentioned probably in an earlier part of this interview, Monroe Burger -- that I heard -- someone had asked me to go hear, and after I listened to a few sets and we left, he said, 'What did you think of him' and I said, 'He dazzled me, but he didn't move me.'
But that was because he had tremendous technique, but, you know, kind of, as we call it, little 'soul'.
